drills.q: Bucket accessed ~once per month, 5TB. Best class and why?
drills.a: Nearline: ~half the storage price of Standard with $0.01/GB retrieval; at monthly access the break-even favors it. Respect 30-day minimum to avoid early-deletion fees.

drills.q: Access pattern unknown across a 50TB mixed bucket. Autoclass or manual lifecycle? Defend.
drills.a: Autoclass: per-object observation beats guessing; waives retrieval/early-deletion fees so misprediction is cheap. Revisit if metrics show uniformly hot data (mgmt fee buys nothing).

drills.q: Explain Spanner commit-wait including why Paxos hides most of it.
drills.a: commit_ts = TT.now().latest; must wait until TT.now().earliest > commit_ts so no later transaction anywhere gets an earlier timestamp. Paxos quorum RTT runs in parallel - residual wait only when quorum finishes inside the eps window (~1-7ms).

drills.q: Fintech audit needs 'trade B definitely executed after trade A' globally. Which DB and which guarantee?
drills.a: Spanner: external consistency/strict serializability backed by hardware-bounded TrueTime. CRDB serializable via HLC does NOT promise cross-node real-time ordering. If staying multi-cloud, state explicitly that wall-clock ordering evidence weakens.

drills.q: Bigtable telemetry table: one node pegged at 100%, cluster idle. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Hot tablet from monotonic keys. Fix schema: hash or salt the leading key component (hash#id#ts), pad IDs; create table with pre-split rows matching key distribution. Scaling nodes adds nothing until keys distribute.

drills.q: Postgres app at 90% CPU on Cloud SQL primary, reads 70% of traffic. Decision path?
drills.a: Read load first: add Cloud SQL replicas (accept lag) or move to AlloyDB read pool for stronger consistency reads. Write/CPU ceilings: AlloyDB disaggregated storage + bigger shapes + columnar engine for any analytical queries. Wire-compatible so no code change.

drills.q: Firestore bill exploded after launch. Three likely causes and fixes.
drills.a: 1) N+1 doc reads -> batch gets/cache. 2) Realtime listeners active on backgrounded screens -> attach/detach lifecycle management. 3) Aggregate queries re-read collections -> scheduled functions writing summary docs. Alert on per-collection read rates.

drills.q: Compliance: objects must survive accidental deletion >=90 days. Layered design?
drills.a: Versioning (prior versions survive overwrite/delete) + soft delete (configurable retention ~) + bucket retention policy 90 days (undeletable before age) + optional retention lock making even admins unable to shorten. Legal holds per object where needed.

drills.q: 200k QPS feature lookups, ms latency, realtime ML serving. Store choice and fallback plan.
drills.a: Bigtable: horizontal node scaling (~10k QPS/node heuristic ~), hashed key prefixes for distribution. Fallback: replication with multi-cluster routing + client cache absorbing gaps; Redis only if dataset fits memory comfortably.

drills.q: 'AlloyDB made our queries 100x faster' - what follow-up questions prove or disprove it?
drills.a: Baseline: tuned PG on fast storage or default config? Which queries - columnar-eligible scans/aggregations or point lookups (row path anyway)? Columnar engine coverage configured for those tables? Data volume warehouse-scale or operational-scale? The claim is benchmark-shaped, not universal.

drills.q: Why is NTP-synchronized clock uncertainty insufficient to replicate Spanner's guarantees outside Google's infrastructure?
drills.a: NTP-only synchronization typically leaves clock uncertainty in the tens-to-hundreds of milliseconds range, versus TrueTime's under-7ms bound from GPS receivers and atomic clocks cross-checked in every datacenter. Commit-wait's cost scales directly with the uncertainty bound being waited out -- at NTP-scale uncertainty, commit-wait would either add unacceptable per-transaction latency or force accepting a materially weaker consistency guarantee than Spanner's. This is why TrueTime-grade external consistency is a genuine infrastructure moat, not just a software technique anyone can replicate by copying the commit-wait algorithm.

drills.q: Explain why Bigtable and BigQuery are often used together for the same clickstream dataset rather than picking one.
drills.a: Bigtable serves the ingestion/serving path: extremely high write throughput, low-latency single-key lookups (e.g. a user's last N events by user_id), no ad-hoc analytical query need. BigQuery serves the analysis path: ad-hoc SQL aggregation, joins, scan-based billing suited to occasional large queries rather than constant point lookups. Bigtable has no SQL engine or secondary indexes, so analytical queries beyond a row-key range scan require either a slow client-side full scan or BigQuery's external Bigtable connector -- worse than querying data already loaded natively into BigQuery. A pipeline (Dataflow) continuously loads the same stream into both, accepting the duplication as the right tradeoff.
